title: A little Easter color at Berlin Farms
summary: Our Easter visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: an egg hunt, bunny photographs, a family album, and a map with practical access and sensory planning notes.

White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. The family storyMap & visit detailsAccess & sensory notesMore photographs Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too. White fences, open fields, and a sky still considering its spring options. One for the albumThe good partis right here.The photographs beside the black door are worth keeping in the set. There is a cap being adjusted, a yellow egg on the grass, and four very large letters spelling LOVE. The farm has helpfully supplied the caption.A tote bag, a bunny, and a few photographs I am glad we took.That is what I want to keep from this Easter visit: the color on the lawn, the bunny pictures, and our family together in the middle of it.One more photograph beside the LOVE door. Ask about the whole route.Our photos show grass, stone paving and a wooden deck. Ask about the route from event parking to check-in, the egg-hunt area and bunny photographs, including steps, slopes and any firm, step-free alternative. Wet-weather arrangements are worth checking before setting out. Check the facilities for that session.Ask which restrooms will be open, whether there is an accessible toilet, and what changing space is available if your family needs it. Check for somewhere to sit and an easy route back to the car. Preview the bunny; keep a choice.A photo of the costume can help make the visit more familiar beforehand. Let each person choose whether to join a photograph, watch, wave or move on. Keep an iPad or other communication support within reach, with an easy way to ask for a break or say “finished.” Ask about crowds, sound and breaks.Find out which session tends to have fewer visitors, whether there will be music or amplified announcements, and where someone can step away. Check re-entry arrangements. Those details are useful to ask about directly when deciding whether the event fits your family.
